China’s oil imports from Iran are collapsing:

China imported ~6.9 million barrels of crude oil per day in the first 20 days of September, near its lowest level in 10 years.

This is well below the ~10.5 million barrels per day China imported on average before the Iran War.

At the same time, Chinese imports of Iranian crude dropped to ~80,000 barrels per day, on track for the 2nd-lowest level in at least 10 years.

This is down -92% to -95% from the 1.0 to 1.5 million barrels per day imported before the war.

As a result, China has imported ~600 million fewer barrels of seaborne oil this year than it would have if it had maintained 2025 import levels.

China is also partially replacing Iranian crude with oil from Iraq, the UAE, Brazil, and Canada.

Iranian oil is disappearing from China’s import mix.

Q: In a recent interview in U.S. News and World Report, Secretary of the Treasury Blumenthal blamed our current rising inflation in large part on our foreign trade and unions. He did, however, say that the government was little to blame. Would you like to comment on that?

Milton Friedman: Yes. Unfortunately it is one of the defects of our political system that we always put a Secretary of the Treasury and other high government officials into a position in which, when they make public statements, they are almost driven, well, what’s the word I want to use? I want to use a polite word: equivocate.

Secretary Blumenthal knows as well as you and I do that inflation does not come from trade unions. That doesn’t mean that trade unions aren’t grasping, of course they are, but they don’t produce inflation for one simple reason. They do not own a printing press on which you can turn out green pieces of paper. The only such printing press is in Washington. I say printing press; of course in the modern age we do it in a more sophisticated way. We use bookkeepers and accountants and computers, but it comes down to the same thing.

Inflation is made in Washington because only Washington can create money, and any other attribution of inflation to other groups is wrong.

Consumers don’t produce it.

Producers don’t produce it.

Trade unions don’t produce it.

Foreign sheiks don’t produce it.

Oil imports don’t produce it.  

What produces it is too much government spending and too much government creation of money, and nothing else.

If they have been voting higher spending and not voting the higher taxes to pay for it, why? Because it’s been politically profitable to do it.

We would all like to get something for nothing. And so the political process has been leading to Congress increasing spending, not increasing taxes, and financing the difference by the hidden tax of inflation. I think we are unwise, but let’s not blame the others. The problem, you know, in that famous statement of a cartoonist: we have met the enemy and they is us.

Jensen may need to update the bottle.

Last year, Jensen Huang famously gave Nscale CEO Josh Payne a bottle of Johnnie Walker inscribed “$0 to $50 billion in 18 months.” With Nscale now reportedly targeting a ~$30-35B IPO valuation, we went through the new $NSCL S-1 to update our $IREN comp.

At that valuation, IREN doesn't look as obviously cheap. On headline backlog multiples, Nscale is actually cheaper.

>Nscale: $30-35B / $103.4B TCV (Total Contract Value) = 0.29-0.34x
>IREN today: ~$20B EV / ~$16B TCV = ~1.25x
>IREN at its YE27 target of 800MW leased / ~$48B TCV = ~0.42x
>At Jensen's $50B marker, IREN looked a bit cheaper on forward TCV: ~0.42x vs ~0.48x. At $30-35B for Nscale, it's the other way around: ~0.29-0.34x vs ~0.42x for IREN.

But there are some pretty big differences in what sits behind those numbers:

Nscale's contracts average 5.7 years vs ~3 years for IREN, so every leased MW naturally produces a lot more TCV. And >80% of Nscale TCV comes from Microsoft + Anthropic, with Anthropic alone accounting for up to $44.6B, or ~43%. IREN is concentrated too: Microsoft is roughly half of its current contracted backlog, but that concentration should fall materially as IREN approaches its 800MW leased target.

The major question is how much infrastructure still needs to materialize to monetize the backlog: Nscale has ~1.37GW of active/contracted capacity today, but fulfilling its $103B TCV requires substantially more power to come online. Its plan to reach 8-10GW also relies heavily on BTM generation, adding cost and execution risk.

The Anthropic contracts are a good example: Nscale says it has no binding commitments for the financing required, Anthropic can terminate a late tranche without liability, and Nscale generally doesn't lock up equipment through long-term supply agreements, instead ordering largely just-in-time.

IREN has the opposite problem. It still needs to lease the capacity, but has >2GW of energized/approved power behind the story already. Its 2026-27 contracted builds are also ~90-95% covered by GPU financing and customer prepayments, although the broader buildout obviously still requires a huge amount of capital.

So Nscale at $30-35B is cheaper on headline forward TCV. The question is how much of a discount that $103B deserves for duration, concentration and the power/financing still required to deliver it.

Good Morning from Germany, where the economy is defying surging energy prices & higher interest rates. Ifo business confidence rose for a 5th straight month to 89.9 in Sep, beating expectations of 89.0. 
Both current conditions and expectations improved as spending on defence and infrastructure starts reaching the economy. Yet all 3 gauges remain well below their long-term averages. A cyclical rebound is taking shape; a structural comeback still needs reforms. 
Taken at face value, the Ifo reading points to GDP growth of ~0.5% QoQ in Q3, acc to Capital Economics; though it doubts actual growth will be that strong.
